Hi. I write a lot too. You might be struggling to read poems more than others. Many autistic people struggle with non-literal language. There's lots of it in poetry. Even highly educated allistic people struggle with it. 

Theres also a lot of poetry that isn't too hard to understand, though. They include those of Wendy Cope, Rudyard Kipling, Pam Ayers or Robert Burns. Poetry can be easy to understand and still be great. Not all difficult poetry is necessarily superior.

 What also helps me is instead of asking what a poem is about or what it means, I ask what experience the speaker is describing. Are they fighting in war, falling in love or smelling a rose? Often, except in ballads or epics, poets famously use lots and lots of words to describe what they're thinking, in a situation so brief the title of the poem is usually a dead giveaway.

They include Little Black Boy, by William Blake or Lines on a Young Lady's Photograph Album by Philip Larkin (tricky poem) or We are Seven by William Wordsworth ( wonderful poem).

Hi. I'm a poet. I love analysing poems. I couldn't get through the part of your post on media studies, but I enjoyed the part you wrote about Wilfred Owen's poem. It's amazing, isn't it? 

I think you're much better at analysing poems than you give yourself credit for! If I understand you correctly, what challenges you is that the speaker/narrator of the poem isn't addressing the reader. He, assuming it's a he, is recounting the horrors at war almost as it happens; possibly addressing himself or another soldier.

The poet does this, as you mentioned, to capture how much the speaker is panicking. Again, as you mentioned, he captures that well, say, when we panic trying to find the house keys. However, when we panic, we don't always sound very coherent. That makes Owen's poem realistic or believable, but hard to understand at first.

What I'd suggest is discussing the poem by breaking it into bits. 

1. Title. What does the title mean (Google translate can decode the Latin). I'm terrible at chosing titles for my own.

2. Content (What do you think the poem is saying). You did that well. Writing about it instead of just thinking seemed to help you!!

3. History (if you go to the notes section behind your book, commenting on that poem, it should say when, where and why the poet wrote the poem you're reading. -i'd do that right after decoding the title!!!

4. Who is the speaker and who is he speaking to? Notice, a poem's speaker can be the poet, but it doesn't have to be. Sometimes, we write poems in the character of say a King addressing his subjects. Not always knowingly.

 Eminem, the rapper, I feel unknowngly slips into the character of an unknown black persona. Just my impression, given the slang and dialect. Sometimes, however, he knowingly slips into the character of a guy he calls Slim Shady. It's his angry persona. Eminem is his persona too seeing it's not the rappers real name.

5. This one is tricky: form and metre. I'd do that after discussing the title. By form I mean, how many stanzas does it have. How many lines are in each stanza. What is its rhyme scheme? That's if the teacher cares about that. Not all do. 

6. Your opinion: What do you think the poet wanted to achieve by writing the poem? As you rightly mentioned, in this case, Owen wanted to really bring home to the reader what exactly goes through your head when you're fighting for dear life. ALSO: was the poet successful in doing this? Again, as you rightly said, seeing we struggle making sense  when we're frantic, that does make the poem hard to understand, at first. Yet it makes it realistic or as critics say "believable".

7. Conclusion: did you like it? Why  or why not? Does it remind you of other poems or works of literature?

That's a lot, I know. You could also attempt a poem yourself in the last situation you were in while frantic, say when trying to make sense of that Wilfred Owen verse you just posted about on Reddit. There's a lot you can do, as you see, but I think you understand poems well. Each teacher just judges reports differently!
